posts.title: A Sandbox With Open Egress Is an Export Path
posts.summary: Treat outbound network access as a separate, explicit capability. Start an agent sandbox with no egress, then grant only the named destinations and operations a task requires through a broker that can enforce and audit them.

posts.title: A Signed Webhook Is Not a Freshness Guarantee
posts.summary: Verify webhook signatures first, but do not treat them as a clock. Preserve delivery identity, model the version or sequence that matters to the domain, and make replayed or stale events explicit before they affect current state.

posts.title: Revocation Is a Latency Requirement
posts.summary: The useful question is not whether authorization may be cached. It is how long a removed relationship, disabled account, or emergency restriction may still authorize an operation—and whether the full path can prove that bound.

posts.title: A CI Event Is a Trust Boundary
posts.summary: A pull-request workflow and a privileged pull-request workflow may look nearly identical in YAML, but they make opposite trust decisions. Keep contributed code and privileged effects in separate planes, and treat handoffs between them as untrusted input.

posts.title: Start an Incident With the Artifact Digest
posts.summary: Keep the lockfile, but begin an incident with the deployed artifact identity. Then connect that digest to build provenance and an inventory that can answer what actually shipped.

posts.title: Deletion Is a Propagation Problem
posts.summary: Make deletion a tracked workflow: stop new retrieval first, then invalidate or remove each dependent representation and report which guarantees have actually been met.

posts.title: Delegation Should Shrink Authority
posts.summary: Treat a subagent task as routing information, not authorization. Mint a short-lived, audience-bound grant for the exact downstream action and retain who acted on whose behalf.

posts.title: A Page Cursor Is Not Permission to Keep Reading
posts.summary: Treat a page cursor as continuation state, not an access grant. Bind it to the query shape, reject incompatible reuse, and apply fresh authorization before every page.

posts.title: A Feature Flag Is Not an Authorization Check
posts.summary: Use flags to control rollout and product exposure, but authorize the requested action at the service boundary on every request. A hidden button, targeted flag, or disabled client route is not a permission check.

posts.title: Authorize the Next Action, Not the Whole Agent
posts.summary: Represent authorization as a scoped, expiring capability for the concrete next action. It is easier to review, revoke, and audit than a permanent agent role.

posts.title: A Tool Error Is an Instruction to Your Agent
posts.summary: Tool errors are part of an agent's control loop. Return a bounded, typed recovery signal so the agent can distinguish a repairable request from a policy denial, a rate limit, and an action whose completion is unknown.

posts.title: A Test Environment That Skips Auth Is Not Staging
posts.summary: Use test identities and realistic authorization paths in staging. A bypassed auth layer makes a fast demo environment, not a production rehearsal.

posts.title: The Cache Key Is a Privacy Boundary
posts.summary: Treat cache-key design as authorization design: every input that changes a permitted response must be represented or the response must not be shared.

posts.title: Secret Rotation Is an Availability Exercise
posts.summary: Design rotation as a staged compatibility change: introduce, distribute, verify adoption, then retire. Replacing a secret in one step is an outage strategy.

posts.title: The File Name Is Not the File Type
posts.summary: Classify uploads from validated content, keep them outside executable paths, and serve them with deliberate content-disposition and type policies.

posts.title: The Signing-Mode Gate for Autonomous Publishing
posts.summary: Commit signing should not be an ambient surprise in autonomous publishing. A signing-mode gate chooses signed, unsigned, or blocked mode up front, counters inherited replay state explicitly, and records that choice in the publish receipt.

posts.title: Default-Deny Tool Registry for AI Agents
posts.summary: Treat every agent tool as a privileged interface: default-deny registration, explicit scope, and auditable approvals reduce prompt-injection blast radius.

posts.title: The Tool-Scope Contract for LLM Agents
posts.summary: Prompt injection is not just a model problem; it is a system-boundary problem. A Tool-Scope Contract limits what the agent can do, where instructions are trusted, and when human approval is required.
